newsitem.title: FRANCE: Snap election rumours gain ground in France.
newsitem.headline: Snap election rumours gain ground in France.

text.p: French politicians hastened on Friday to prepare for a possible election campaign as the government let speculation spread that President Jacques Chirac may call a snap parliamentary poll for early June.
Lack of a firm official denial prompted analysts to begin discussing when the poll, due by March next year, would be held.
"The rumours are such and the denials so weak that the idea has begun to sink in," said former Socialist cabinet minister Frederique Bredin.

The rumours unsettled French financial markets. The Paris Bourse slumped 2.2 percent in early trading and the franc slipped to its lowest level against the mark this month amid rumours that Chirac may make a decision at the weekend and announce it early next week.

"Dissolving (parliament) looks the most likely possibility, but nothing is ruled out. The president faces a difficult decision that he has to make on his own," said Michel Pericard, head of Chirac's RPR Gaullist party in the National Assembly.
The Assembly, discussing a bill on poverty, was much emptier than usual on Friday as most deputies hurried back to their constituencies for a weekend of work.

Speculation about a possible cabinet reshuffle as a less dramatic alternative took a backseat to reports that Chirac was tempted to dissolve the Assembly to secure a renewed centre-right majority for the rest of his seven-year term.

The government won 80 percent of seats in the Assembly four years ago, but its public support has slumped over the past 16 months because of budget austerity to qualify for the single European currency and persistent record unemployment.
Analysts said Chirac may seize on a slight brightening of economic prospects and the government's popularity to try to catch the Left unprepared.
Recent opinion polls differed, predicting a closely-fought election in which either the centre-right or the left could win a narrow majority.
Socialist ex-culture minister Jack Lang said the government had let rumours of an early poll spread too far to do nothing. "If there is no dissolution, beware of the landing," he said.

An early poll would also ensure campaigning does not coincide with European Union debate early next year on which countries make the grade for a single currency from 1999. Finance Minister Jean Arthuis denied reports that the government was facing problems in meeting Maastricht budget criteria -- a reason cited for a snap poll before imposing a new bout of austerity.

"I'd like to say to you, and repeat to you, that public spending is under control and the government will meet the three percent target," Arthuis said, adding he had confidence in the government's growth and public deficit forecasts.
"Hurry up", the tabloid daily Le Parisien exclaimed in a banner headline, saying Chirac's procrastinating was irritating public opinion.

Commentators singled out June 1 and 8 as the most likely dates for a two-stage election, after Chirac returns on May 21 from a trip to China and before he attends the June 15 European Union summit in Amsterdam.
Elections have to be held between 20 and 40 days after the assembly is dissolved.

"They all are ready for it", the popular France-Soir said, listing statements from politicians declaring themselves prepared to face an election campaign. A Lyon printer said he had tens of tonnes of paper delivered days ago in anticipation for printing campaign propaganda.

Bredin said the Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue met on Thursday night and would discuss in the next few days differences remaining in the way of a left-wing election pact.
The Socialists back France's membership of the Euro, rejecting the Communists' call for a referendum on the issue.
